answer.rationale: Three signals converge on the recent release as the most probable cause: (1) the p99 write-path degradation is confined to the primary region and began within the window after the release went out 2 hours ago, matching the pattern in memory_b1 where a bad release produced a checkout error spike that was immediately cleared by rollback with no customer impact. (2) Settlement traffic is at daily peak and writes are heavy, meaning the write path is under maximum stress—any release-induced regression will compound quickly and risk sustained write loss if left to escalate. (3) Regional failover (memory_b2) is tempting given the region-confined pattern, but failover would move live settlement writes at peak volume to a region that has not been proven under this exact load profile; that introduces a second failure mode (capacity mismatch on the standby) while leaving the defective build in place. Add_capacity would not address a code-level regression. Enabling a circuit breaker or routing reads to replicas does not target the write path, which is where the degradation is manifesting. Rolling back the release is the narrowest, fastest intervention that removes the most likely root cause while preserving all in-flight writes (the prior build is known stable per memory_b1) and avoids the blast-radius risk of shifting peak settlement traffic across regions. After the rollback completes and latency recovers, the next window can be used to (a) investigate whether the release interacted with peak settlement volume in a way that regional failover would not have solved either, and (b) assess whether canary gating (memory_b6) should be tightened so this class of regression is caught pre-GA.
